transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi, nice to meet you too. Um, well, it's... it's a lot of things, I guess, but what finally made me make the appointment—what really scared me enough to actually come in today—is just... where my mind has been going lately. 

I work as a veterinary technologist, and I’ve been doing it for years, since I finished my degree, and it's always demanding work. You're on your feet, dealing with sick animals, stressed owners, the whole thing. But lately, I just... I keep having this recurring thought when I go to bed that it would just be so much easier if I simply didn't wake up the next morning. Just, you know, if it all just stopped and I didn't have to do any of it anymore. 

And then... well, the commute is what really pushed me to call. I have this drive home from the clinic every evening, and it's the exact same route I've taken a thousand times, but recently, I'll be driving, taking a curve, and I catch myself just staring at the road and wondering... what would happen if I just didn't turn the wheel? Like, if I just let my hands drop and let the car keep going straight. It's not like I'm sitting there mapping it out, but the fact that the thought is just casually sitting there in my head, almost like it's a reasonable option... it really terrified me. I realized I couldn't just brush it off anymore.
Right now, do you want to die?

I... I don't know if I *want* to die. That feels like such a strong way to put it, you know? Like, wanting to die implies I have this whole plan and I'm actively trying to make it happen, and I'm not. But... it's just like I was saying about the car. It's more of this overwhelming feeling that it would just be so much easier if it all just stopped. 

Like, when I'm lying in bed, exhausted from being on my feet all day at the clinic, dealing with the animals and the owners—who, by the way, can be so demanding and ungrateful sometimes, even when you're doing everything you can to save their pet—I just lie there and think, "What if I just didn't wake up?" It wouldn't be painful. It wouldn't be messy. It would just be... quiet. No more alarms, no more rushing, no more of this heavy, awful feeling dragging me down every single day. 

And then there's the drive home. I've been driving that same stretch of road for years, I know every pothole and every curve, but lately, it's like my hands just feel so heavy on the steering wheel. I'll be coming up to that one sharp bend right past the old oak tree—you know, the one where the road narrows a bit—and my brain just whispers, "What if you just let go? What if you just let the car go straight?" It's not that I'm stepping on the gas trying to crash, but the thought is just there, hovering, making me wonder if slipping away wouldn't be the worst thing in the world. So, no, I don't think I *want* to die, but I am so, so tired of being alive like this, and that's what terrifies me.
Have you been finding it hard to enjoy things that you usually care about?

Yeah, actually, that's... that's a big part of what's been so upsetting. It's like all the color has just drained out of everything. I used to be so passionate about things outside of work, you know? Like, my photography. I have this really nice DSLR camera that I saved up for, and I used to take it out every weekend. I'd go to the state park, or even just walk around the neighborhood, trying to catch the light just right, especially in the early morning when the dew is still on the grass. I haven't even taken it out of its case in... I don't even know how long. It's just sitting there on the shelf in my office, gathering dust. 

And the birds, too. I have these three different feeders set up in the backyard—one for suet, a tube feeder for the finches, and a platform one—and I used to love sitting by the window with my coffee, just watching them and logging the different species that would visit. I knew exactly when the cardinals would show up, and I’d make sure the squirrel baffle was working. But now... I mean, I still fill them, I guess, because I feel guilty if they go hungry, but I don't actually care to watch them anymore. I just dump the seed in and walk away. 

Even my garden... I usually spend the whole winter planning out what I'm going to plant, sketching out the beds, ordering seeds from these specialty catalogs. But this year, I haven't even looked at a catalog. I couldn't care less what blooms or doesn't bloom. And it's just... it's frightening, honestly. Those things—the camera, the birds, the garden—those were the things that made me feel like *me*. They were my escape from the stress at the clinic. And now that I don't care about them, it's like... I don't even know who I am without them. It's just this heavy, blank feeling where all my interests used to be.
How long have you been feeling this way?

Well, it's... it's been a really long time, honestly. I've been trying to pinpoint exactly when it started, because you know how these things are, they sort of creep up on you without you really noticing until you're completely submerged. But if I really think back, this... this dark cloud, this heavy depression, it’s been hanging over me for about 11 months now. 

I remember it was right around the end of spring last year. We had this huge influx of parvo cases at the clinic, which is always just devastating and exhausting, and usually I bounce back after a tough stretch like that. But I just didn't. I kept waiting to feel normal again, waiting to want to go out and take pictures or care about my garden, and it just never happened. I spent the whole summer and fall just dragging myself out of bed, going through the motions at work, and coming home to just collapse. 

And then, I don't know, it's like this past month, something shifted and it just got so much worse. That's when the thoughts about the car and not waking up really started to take hold. It was bad enough for those first ten months, just feeling empty and tired all the time, but this last month... it's like the volume got turned way up on everything awful. It just feels completely unbearable now. I can't keep doing this if it's going to stay like this. It's just been going on for so long. Eleven months is a long time to feel like you're just a ghost in your own life, you know?
Right before this started about 11 months ago, did something significant happen in your life that felt like a major stressor or change?

I've thought about that a lot, actually. You know, trying to figure out the "why" of it all. Because it seems like there should be a reason, right? Like, a catalyst. A sudden death in the family, or a terrible breakup, or getting fired. Something you can point to and say, "There, that's when everything went wrong." But... no, there wasn't anything like that. 

I mean, I mentioned the parvo outbreak at the clinic, and yes, that was stressful. It's always stressful when you have puppies coming in so sick, and you have to do all the barrier nursing—the gowns, the gloves, the bleach footbaths—and you're just praying they make it through the night. And the owners are usually so distraught, crying in the waiting room, and you have to be the strong one, explaining the IV fluids and the anti-nausea meds and the antibiotics, trying to give them hope without making false promises. It takes a toll, it really does. I've been a vet tech for almost thirty years, and it never gets easier to watch an animal suffer. 

But... that's just the job. It's what I do. I've been through dozens of outbreaks like that over the years. We had a terrible bout of feline panleukopenia back in 2018 that nearly broke the whole staff, but even then, I bounced back. I was tired, sure, but I didn't fall into this... this black hole. 

So, no, there wasn't any big, catastrophic event right before this started. My life was completely normal. Routine, even. I was getting up, going to work, coming home, feeding the birds, planning the garden... just doing all the things I've always done. There was no major fight with a friend, no financial crisis, no health scare... nothing. And honestly, I think that makes it worse. Because if there was a reason, maybe I could fix it, you know? If it was grief, I could go to a grief counselor. If it was a bad breakup, time would heal it. But because there's no reason... it just feels like my brain broke for absolutely no cause at all. It just decided to stop working right one day in the middle of spring, and I've been stuck like this ever since.
Before this depression started about 11 months ago, was there ever another period in your life when you felt depressed like this for weeks or months at a time?

No, honestly, I... I don't think so. I mean, I've had periods where I was sad, sure. Everyone gets sad. I remember when my first dog, Buster, passed away—he was a golden retriever mix, the absolute sweetest boy, I adopted him right after I finished my tech program. When he died, I cried for days. I was a mess for a couple of weeks, just walking into the house and expecting to hear his nails on the hardwood floor, you know? But that was grief. That made sense. I still wanted to eat, I still went to work, even if I was teary-eyed in the breakroom. 

And there have been stressful times, like I mentioned with the clinic, where I'd come home exhausted and just want to sleep all weekend. But it never felt like this. It never felt like this heavy, suffocating blanket that just won't lift. I've always been a pretty steady person, I think. I've always been able to find joy in my hobbies, in the animals, in the little things. I've never had a time where the color just drained out of everything for months on end. 

I've been racking my brain, trying to think if maybe in my twenties or thirties there was a time like this, but... no. I've always been the reliable one, the one who shows up for her shift, the one who keeps the garden looking nice. This... this emptiness, this total inability to care about anything, and these dark thoughts... it's all completely new. And that's part of why it's so terrifying. If I had been through it before, maybe I'd know how to handle it, or at least know that it eventually ends. But because it's never happened before, I just feel completely lost in it. I don't know how to navigate this version of myself. It's like I'm a stranger in my own body, and I've never felt like this stranger before in my entire fifty-two years.
